The lab exercise is carried out using [R](https://www.r-project.org/) and the [lidR-package](https://github.com/r-lidar/lidR). The [lidRBook](https://r-lidar.github.io/lidRbook/) is a fantastic resource! 

# _**Intro area-based approach**_

The basic steps of the area-based method are as follows [@Naesset2014-dy]:

1. Stand delineation and interpretation: The forest stands in the area of interest (AOI) are delineated. Delineation using orthophotos or stereo photogrammery is commonly adopted. Manual interpretation is conducted to derive properties like for example tree species, site quality, and age which are required either as primary variables that are sought for every stand in the inventory or used for stratification of the inventory.

2. Sample survey: A field sample survey is conducted across the entire AOI. Such surveys are commonly performed according to stratified sampling schemes applying systematic sampling with a random start or systematic cluster sampling. Thus, the collected sample of field plots can be considered as a (stratified) probability sample. Conventional field data are collected on the plots (e.g. tree diameter and height) and the plots are accurately geo-referenced.

3. ALS acquisition and processing: ALS data are acquired for the AOI. The entire AOI is partitioned into regular grid cells with cell size equal to the sample plot size. Various metrics are derived from the 3D ALS point cloud for each cell and field plot. These metrics basically belong to two distinct “families” of variables, namely (1) canopy height-related variables like order statistics, mean height, and variability among the heights of the ALS echoes and (2) canopy density metrics which characterize the frequency of echoes above a certain height threshold relative to the total number of recorded echoes. A wide range of other metrics or slightly modified metrics can be found in the literature.

4. Model fitting: Based on the sample plots regression models with biophysical properties such as mean height, basal area and volume as dependent variables are fitted with ALS metrics used as independent variables.

5. Stand-wise estimation: Finally, the fitted models are used to predict the biophysical properties of interest for every grid cell. The individual cell estimates are aggregated to stand estimates.

This lab will focus on steps 3 and 4. 



# _**Part 1: Compute point cloud metrics**_

## Read and normalize point cloud data 

The following code reads a rectangle of the 2021 LAZ file from Frydenhaug and extract a "field plot" located on UTM32 East 600080 North 6615950 of 400 m². 

```{r}
library(lidR)
lasFile <- "data/frydenhaug/als2021.laz" # Filename
filter <- "-keep_xy 599850 6615750 600250 6616030 -keep_class 1 2" # ALS returns inside a boundary, only class 1 (unclassified), and 2 (ground)
lasdata <- readLAS(lasFile,filter=filter)
lasdz <- normalize_height(lasdata, tin())
las <- clip_circle(lasdz, 600080, 6615950, radius = sqrt(400/pi))
plot(las)
```

The las-file attributes can be access as in a standard data.frame.

```{r}
plot(las$X,las$Z,asp=1) #asp = setting the X Y axes equal
#Make pretty plot
source("R/laser.colors.R") # Reads in a predefined function 
plot(las$X,las$Z,asp=1,pch=".",col=laser.colors(las$Z)) #asp = setting the X Y axes equal
# Threshold of 2 m "The Nilsson rule" :-)
plot(las$X,las$Z,col=ifelse(las$Z>=2,"green","red"),asp=1,pch=".")
abline(h=2)
```
## Height metrics 

Compute mean height with a threshold >= 2 m

```{r}
Hmean <- mean(las$Z[las$Z>=2])
Hmean # To print could also have used () before and after expression above
```

> **_TASK:_**  Compute standard deviation of height (function *sd*), height percentiles (function *quantile*) and coefficient of variation cv = sd/mean

```{r}
(Hsd <- sd(las$Z[las$Z>=2]))

(Hcv <- Hsd/Hmean)

seq(0,1,0.05) # To create a sequence of numbers ?seq for info
q <- quantile(las$Z[las$Z>=2],probs=seq(0,1,0.05))
names(q) <- paste("H",seq(0,1,0.05)*100,sep="")
paste0("H",seq(0,1,0.05)*100)

```


## Density metrics 

Compute density metrics D0 and D9 with a threshold >= 2 m.
```{r}
ntot <- length(las$Z) # or nrow(las)
nabove <- length(las$Z[las$Z>=2])
(D0 = nabove/ntot)

ntot <- length(las$Z)# nrow(las)
H95 <- quantile(las$Z[las$Z>=2],probs=0.95)
layer <- (((H95 - 2)/10 )*9)+2
nabove <- length(las$Z[las$Z>=layer])
(D9 = nabove/ntot)
```

Implement for all density metrics 

```{r}
layers <-  c(0:9)*(quantile(las$Z[las$Z >= 2], probs=0.95) - 2)/10 + 2
density.metrics <- c()
for(i in c(1:10)){
  ntot <- length(las$Z)# nrow(las)
  nabove <- length(las$Z[las$Z>=layers[i]])
  density.metrics[i] <- nabove/ntot
}
density.metrics

```

## Compute metrics for different echo categories 

> **_TASK:_**  The standard approach in the area-based methods is to separate metrics based on first and last echoes. Compute the metrics above for the two different types of echos (returns). Hint use variables ReturnNumber and NumberOfReturns. First returns (first of many + single) ReturnNumber == 1 and Last returns (last of many) ReturnNumber == NumberOfReturns & ReturnNumber != 1    


```{r}
# Filter first of many and single - 3 different ways to obtain the same result
names(las) # List the different attributes
first <- filter_first(las)
dim(first)
first <- filter_poi(las, ReturnNumber == 1)
dim(first)
first <- las[las$ReturnNumber == 1]
dim(first)
```

```{r}
#Filter last
last <- filter_last(las) #Last of many and single!!!!!
dim(last)
last <- filter_poi(las, ReturnNumber == NumberOfReturns & ReturnNumber != 1) # Only Last of many
dim(last)
```

> **_TASK:_**  Do the same for the image matching point cloud dap2021.las

## Compute all metrics using a predefined function

In lidR there exists functions to calculate point cloud metrics e.g. *stdmetrics_z*. Explanation of metrics computed using the *stdmetrics_z* function can be found [here](https://github.com/r-lidar/lidR/wiki/stdmetrics). I have provided a function for the point cloud metrics discussed that follow the Norwegian tradition and the implementation of [@Naesset2008-cd] . 

```{r}
source("R/stdmetricsNOR.R") # Function computing point cloud metrics the after the Norwegian tradition [@Naesset2008-cd]
dat <- cloud_metrics(las,func=~stdmetricsNOR(Z))
data.frame(dat)
```



# _**Part 2: Area-based approach**_

## Read and inspect laser data
```{r}
library(lidR)
lasFile <- "data/vaaler/las/0008.las"
filter <- "-keep_xy 606200 6600150 606500 6600450" 
las <- readLAS(lasFile,filter=filter)
table(las$Classification)
```

## Normalizing ALS data

```{r}
lasdz <- normalize_height(las, tin())
table(lasdz$Classification)
lasdz_no_noise <- classify_noise(lasdz,algorithm=ivf(5,2)) # classify returns associated to noise in class 18
table(lasdz_no_noise$Classification)
lasdz_filtered <- filter_poi(lasdz_no_noise,Classification != 7 & Classification != 18) # 7 and 18: noise
plot(lasdz_filtered,color="Classification")
plot(lasdz_filtered)
```



## Compute metrics
```{r}
grd <- pixel_metrics(lasdz_filtered,func = ~stdmetricsNOR(Z),res=sqrt(250),filter= ~ReturnNumber == 1)
head(grd)
plot(grd)
plot(grd$H95)
```
## Processing multiple files 

Point clouds are commonly distributed in the form of multiple files that cover specific areas. Each of these files corresponds to a square-shaped region, often referred to as a "tile," and typically has a size of around 200MB. The lidR package provides a comprehensive set of tools for efficiently managing and processing such data. It employs a tile processing system known as a "catalog" to help users navigate and gain an overview of the individual files.


```{r}
ctg <- readLAScatalog("data/vaaler/las/")
plot(ctg)
ctg
```

## Normalize ALS data from multiple files

This take some time, maybe use the skip this step and use data from "data/vaaler/lasdz/"

```{r,eval=FALSE}
ctg <- readLAScatalog("data/vaaler/las/")
opt_filter(ctg) <- "-keep_classification 0 1 2"
opt_output_files(ctg) <-  paste0("data/vaaler/dz/", "/{ORIGINALFILENAME}_norm")
# Not run ctgdz <- normalize_height(ctg, tin())
```


## Extract metrics for reference data

```{r}
library(sf)
library(lidR)
ctgdz <- readLAScatalog("data/vaaler/lasdz/")
plot(ctgdz)
st_layers("data/vaaler/sample_plots.gpkg") # list different layers in gpkg
sample_plots <- read_sf("data/vaaler/sample_plots.gpkg","field_plots")
head(sample_plots)
plot(sample_plots,add=T)
```


```{r,message=FALSE,error=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Function to process the las-catalog using the stdmetricsNOR function for each sample plot of 250 m^2
sqrt(250/pi) # Compute radius of plot 
options(lidR.progress = FALSE)
plots <- plot_metrics(ctgdz, ~stdmetricsNOR(Z), sample_plots, radius = 8.92)
head(plots)

# #Example of 2 plots
# P1 <- lidR::clip_roi(ctgdz, sample_plots[sample_plots$ID=="P1",], radius = 8.92)
# P5 <- lidR::clip_roi(ctgdz, sample_plots[sample_plots$ID=="P5",], radius = 8.92)
# plot(P1)
# plot(P5)
```

## Create regression models

Below we create the regression model for top height (TH)

```{r}
modTH <- lm(TH~H95,data=plots)
summary(modTH)
plot(plots$H95,plots$TH)
abline(coef(modTH))
```

Modelling volume (V) is often done using on variable describing height and one describing the density. 

```{r}
modV <- lm(V~Hmean+D5,data=plots)
summary(modV)
plot(plots$Hmean,plots$V)
```

## Side note on modeling

A more proper modeling approach. log-log models are often used in the area-based approach to linearize the relationships. However, when back transforming *exp(pred)* a bias is introduce. Thus, with computers nowadays nonlinear models can be used while still doing variable selection in the log-log space

```{r}
library(leaps)
library(ggplot2)
dat <- subset(plots, select=c(V,Hmax:Hcv,H10:D9))
dat <- st_drop_geometry(dat)
head(dat)
Xy <- log(dat)
mod <- lm(V~.,data=Xy)
summary(mod)

# Step wise model selection
stepmod <- step(mod,trace=0) 
summary(stepmod) # To many variables 

# Best subset nmax Indicate largest model
reg <- regsubsets(V~.,data=Xy,nvmax=3,really.big=TRUE) 
summary(reg)
mod <- lm(V~H70+D2,data=Xy)
summary(mod)

# Fitting the nonlinear version of the log-log model
mod <- nls(V~b0*H70^b1*D2^b2,data=dat,start=c(b0=1,b1=1,b2=1))
summary(mod)
```

```{r,message=FALSE,error=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# opt_output_files(ctgdz) <- "data/vaaler/metrics/{ORIGINALFILENAME}_metrics" #Output directory NB files exist in downloaded data.

metrics_w2w <- do.call(mosaic, rasters)

```



```{r}
#Do predictions 
library(terra)
plot(metrics_w2w$H95)
TH_pred <- predict(metrics_w2w, modTH) # Predicting top height
plot(TH_pred)

```



